items.title: Distilling World Action Models for Efficient Bimanual Manipulation via Anchored Path Matching
items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step teacher.Project page: https://jialonglong.github.io/Anchored-Path-Matching/.

items.title: Autonomous Track Racing with a Commercially Available Humanoid: System Design and Real-World Deployment
items.summary: Learning-based methods now let humanoids run robustly, and they have begun to compete in athletic events. Yet few reports describe a complete autonomous humanoid running system in an actual race, where the robot must follow a lane at a new venue, pace itself within hardware limits, and finish without intervention. We report such a system deployed on the Unitree G1, a commercially available general-purpose humanoid, in the 100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m events of the World Humanoid Robot Games 2026. The system integrates vision-based lane perception, path tracking, and a running policy trained by reinforcement learning with a human motion prior. To address the challenges of humanoid running, we stabilize head-camera images against body motion and use IMU-assisted leg odometry to bridge flight phases. To manage motor heating, we penalize hip-pitch torque during training, add heat-dissipation plates, and apply temperature-based speed limiting with event-specific pacing. The robot placed 13th of 74 in the 100 m, 10th of 44 in the 400 m first round before falling in the semifinal, and seventh of 35 in the 1500 m. In this deployment, thermal margin set the pace in every event, and the semifinal fall followed a lane-detection error.

items.title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
items.summary: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

items.title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

items.title: Making the World React Realistically: A Closed-Loop Interactive World Model for Autonomous Driving
items.summary: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.

items.title: FailureGen: Scalable Robot Failure Data Generation with World Models
items.summary: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.

items.title: VLM-guided Grounding Expert for Generalised Referring Expression Comprehension
items.summary: Generalised referring expression comprehension (GREC) aims to identify and localise the zero, one or multiple objects referred to by a language expression. In robotic manipulation, grounding also needs to remain accurate when requests for the same objects are paraphrased or embedded in additional context in robotics. However, grounding expert models are sensitive to instruction variation, while generative vision--language models (VLMs) struggle with complete target recovery and rejection of absent targets. These complementary limitations motivate combining the contextual representations of VLMs with the direct spatial prediction capabilities of grounding experts. We therefore introduce VLM-guided Grounding Expert (VGE), which combines a frozen VLM with a trainable grounding expert through layerwise joint attention and text-conditioned instance scoring. These interfaces leverage multimodal understanding of the VLM to guide object-query refinement and candidate selection while retaining direct bounding-box prediction. Across three datasets, VGE achieves the highest averaged F1 score among the evaluated methods on all five test splits, with differences of at most 1.2 percentage points across instruction conditions within each split. On the dataset with robotic scenes, VGE also achieves the highest F1 across instruction variants and no-target, single-target and multiple-target cases. VGE provides a $5.3$--$13.0\times$ inference speedup over the baseline with the same VLM base model. These results support combining VLM context with specialised spatial prediction to address both grounding challenges, with particularly strong performance in robotic scenes. Code will be released upon publication.

items.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
items.summary: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

items.title: Body Schema Policy: Body as the Vision-Action Interface for Efficient Robot Loco-Manipulation
items.summary: Currently, robots can learn whole-body loco-manipulation through scale: the strongest policies have billions of parameters and still need task-specific fine-tuning. Humans have limited processing capacity, yet learn and act efficiently through a body schema that organizes what they see and how they move. We introduce Body Schema Policy (BSP), an imitation learning policy that builds such a schema into the vision-action interface. Its latent body schema places joint and link tokens on the robot's kinematic tree, where learned screw motions carry features between links. Through body-queried vision, each body part retrieves its own visual evidence, which conditions the denoising of its actions. With this inductive bias, BSP returns an action chunk faster than any policy we compare. Compact, body-specific visual readouts also emerge without spatial supervision: manipulation commands depend strongly on task objects, while locomotion commands respond more broadly to the scene. On nine simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tasks, BSP matches the $Ψ_0$ humanoid foundation model with $75\times$ fewer parameters and nearly doubles Diffusion Policy's success. The same holds on a real G1 and a Fetch mobile manipulator.

items.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
items.summary: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

items.title: Risk Density RRT$^*$: Planning in the Space of Probability
items.summary: Planning under uncertainty is a fundamental problem in robotics. While much of the literature seeks minimum-cost paths subject to probabilistic constraints, this paper instead considers collision probability, or risk classically defined as probability times severity, directly as the planning objective. We propose Risk Density RRT$^*$ (RD-RRT$^*$), an extension of RRT$^*$ for high-level planning in environments with deterministic and uncertain obstacles. RD-RRT$^*$ builds on Risk Density, a functional that evaluates a continuous path as a whole and provides a tractable approximation of its collision probability. The framework also supports severity-weighted risk and a hybrid variant that adds a path-length penalty, balancing risk and geometric efficiency while regularizing exploration in low-density regions. We validate the method across a wide range of scenarios. The results show that RD-RRT$^*$ consistently finds paths with lower estimated collision probability by optimizing a global risk-based objective. We further demonstrate the fidelity of the underlying approximation through Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we discuss how the topological structure induced by Risk Density may provide a useful representation of the environment and offer insights into risk-aware planning.

items.title: Plenty to FRET About: From Hazard Analysis to Formal Requirements for Robot-Assisted Dressing
items.summary: Understanding requirements for systems involving humans and robots is essential for providing robust evidence that such systems behave correctly. Requirements formalisation approaches such as the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET) can support the transition from unstructured natural language to formal representations suitable for verification. In this paper, we formalise 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing (RAD) case study, previously classified using a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements. Through an iterative process involving domain-expert clarification, these were represented by 117 unique FRETISH requirements. Formalisation exposed ambiguities, temporal and probabilistic assumptions, and cases where source requirements needed to be decomposed or could be consolidated because they expressed the same formal behaviour. Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. We report practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements and identify directions for further work.

items.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis

items.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours
items.summary: As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43-53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.

items.title: DGV-DLIVO: Degeneracy-Guided Visual Fusion for Direct LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry in Degenerate Tunnel Environments
items.summary: Reliable localization in long underground infrastructures remains a major challenge for autonomous inspection robots. In hydropower spillway tunnels and drainage galleries, repetitive geometric structures provide insufficient constraints along the tunnel axis, while weak texture and illumination variations further degrade visual estimation. Under this coupled degradation, existing LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial odometry systems may lose the ability to recover continuous longitudinal motion. This paper presents DGV-DLIVO, a degeneracy-guided visual fusion for direct LiDAR-inertial-visual odometry for extreme tunnel environments. Instead of treating vision as a general complementary sensor, the proposed method exploits the LiDAR-degenerate direction as an active guidance signal to determine informative visual regions, establish LiDAR-anchored visual associations, and perform subspace-selective fusion. The visual constraints are introduced only into the deficient motion subspace, while unreliable LiDAR information in the same direction is adaptively suppressed and reliable geometric constraints are preserved. Real-world experiments in hydropower tunnels demonstrate that representative state-of-the-art LIO, LIVO, and VIO methods suffer from stagnation, oscillation, severe under-travel, curved drift, or divergence, whereas DGV-DLIVO maintains continuous and directionally consistent tunnel-axis motion estimation under both cart-mounted and handheld acquisition. It achieves a 91.4% progress ratio over the 40m tunnel sequence and significantly improves longitudinal recovery and trajectory stability. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of degeneracy-guided adaptive fusion for robotic inspection in severely degraded underground environments. The source code and a supplementary video are publicly available at https://github.com/0RayZhang0/DGV-DLIVO.

items.title: Progress Predicts Policy
items.summary: A task specifies how the world should change, while a policy specifies what the robot should do. We introduce Progress Predicts Policy (PPP), which learns a language-conditioned scalar field through the commands induced by its differential. We obtain action conditioning by composing a latent progress field with a shared world model and read its action gradient at a fixed reference command. Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar. This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search. Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands. PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field's local control geometry. Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation. The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution. Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.

items.title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.

items.title: DGF-Asym: Adaptive Peer Weighting for Collective Estimation under Noisy and Faulty Sensing
items.summary: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.

items.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $π_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.

items.title: The Multivariate Feedback Particle Filter for State-dependent Multiplicative Noises and Its Application to Attitude and Pose Estimations
items.summary: Nonlinear filtering with state-dependent multiplicative measurement noise poses a notable challenge for spacecraft attitude determination and robotic pose estimation. This work develops the FPF-DM, a decomposition scheme for feedback particle filters tailored to this family of filtering problems. Extending prior decomposition techniques for additive noise and polynomial measurement models, the proposed method resolves the key difficulty that state-dependent multiplicative noise breaks the polynomial assumption and prevents Hermite spectral backward recursion for the weighted Poisson's equation. By measure transformation and importance reweighting, we incorporate the inverse measurement covariance into particle weights and rescale the feedback gain to restore the polynomial-form Poisson's equation, with the decomposition generalized to non-uniformly weighted mixtures for closed-form gain computation. This general FPF-DM is instantiated on quaternion and dual-quaternion manifolds for attitude tracking and point-cloud registration. Simulations on 4D attitude tracking and 8D point-cloud registration verify that the instantiated filters using only 10 particles achieve superior accuracy and computational performance relative to baseline filters.

items.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

items.title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
items.summary: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâserver topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâserver pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

items.title: InteractVLA: Turning VLAs into Interactive Tools for Agentic Robotic Manipulation
items.summary: Existing agentic manipulation systems treat pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies as opaque, language-only primitives: when a policy call fails under unfamiliar instructions or scene perturbations, the agent cannot steer its behavior and is forced into futile retries or costly manual takeover. We present InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools through a bidirectional geometric interface with vision-language agents. In the forward direction, test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, while soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index to match the target pose without distorting the policy's approach motion. In the reverse direction, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent, allowing it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments on top of the guided trajectory. Making the VLA controllable not only boosts online agentic tool use, but also unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), achieving state-of-the-art performance of 99.4\% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62\% on RoboDojo, and 89.4\% on RoboCasa365. items.summary: Human data can support robot policy pretraining, but gains attributed to a data recipe may also reflect subset size, training variability, or downstream adaptation. items.title: Learning Accurate End-Effector Trajectory Tracking with Inertial Feedback for a Quadruped Manipulator
items.summary: Accurate end-effector trajectory tracking on quadruped manipulators is challenging because uncertainties in actuators, foot-ground contact, and geometric errors are propagated through the leg-arm kinematic chain. Detecting such errors requires sensing beyond joint encoders that can capture the effects of these uncertainties on the robot's motion, since joint encoders only provide measurements at the actuated joints and cannot fully observe mechanical errors such as backlash, dimensional inaccuracies, or structural deformation. This work addresses these challenges using a reinforcement learning framework with end-effector (EE) inertial feedback, targeting local high-accuracy manipulation while maintaining a nominal body pose and support configuration without intentional body motion or foot repositioning. The learned policy uses EE inertial measurements to compensate for tracking errors induced by uncertainties throughout the leg-arm system that cannot be fully inferred from proprioception alone. Simulation and real-world experiments on continuous EE trajectory tracking show overall improvements relative to nominal and proprioception-only baselines. In real-world experiments, the proposed policy reduces the MoCap-based RMSE by 17.3% and 28.0% relative to the nominal baseline under the two in-distribution (ID) command conditions, respectively, and by an additional 12.6% and 15.9% relative to the proprioception-only baseline. Furthermore, the trajectory-wise RMSE between FK-reconstructed and motion-capture-measured end-effector positions averaged 12.61+-2.15mm (mean+-standard deviation) across 24 controller-trajectory combinations, revealing a substantial discrepancy between nominal kinematic reconstruction and measured end-effector motion.

items.title: COAST: Safe Flight Corridor Planner for Fast and Robust Snap Minimized Trajectories
items.summary: Current B-Spline trajectory planners face a critical trade-off: they either sacrifice computational speed to maintain strict Safe Flight Corridor (SFC) guarantees, or they abandon hard safety bounds in favor of soft-constraint penalties to achieve real-time performance. We present COAST (Corridor-Optimized Aerially-Safe Trajectories), a B-Spline based, online trajectory planner capable of formulating snap minimized trajectories with SFC guarantees. COAST divides the problem into two stages: an A* based front-end that generates geometrically simple SFCs (represented as a chain of rectangular prisms), and a quadratic programming back-end for control point optimization. To handle the non-convexity of SFC intersections, we leverage the finite support property of B-Splines, to ensure the spline never exits SFC boundaries. The control point optimization incorporates MINVO transforms for kinodynamic bounding, allowing COAST to design non-conservative, dynamically feasible trajectories, while a snap minimization matrix calculation provides flight smoothness. This formulation provides a formal geometric containment guarantee, while ensuring mean trajectory computation times under 5 ms for real-time deployment. We validate our results through high-fidelity simulation experiments. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/byu-magicc/Minimum-Snap-Trajectories

items.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
items.summary: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

items.title: BehaVerify: A Formal Verification Tool for Behavior Trees
items.summary: This paper presents BehaVerify, a verification toolbox for behavior trees (BTs) and Neuro-Symbolic BTs. BTs are a graphical language for planning and sequencing behaviors - similar to extended state machines - and are increasingly used in safety-critical domains. BehaVerify enables users to specify a BT using a Domain Specific Language (DSL) with formal syntax and semantics. This language further includes Linear Temporal Logic and Computation Tree Logic specifications. BehaVerify uses an efficient encoding into nuXmv, called fastforwarding, to quickly verify if a specification holds over the BT. Additionally, BehaVerify can generate implementations of the BT in Python and Haskell. Through Python, BehaVerify has been integrated with PyTrees and Robot Operating System (ROS) and has been deployed to several autonomous robotic systems, including for verifying runtime monitors. While prior works have developed the underlying theory, this manuscript focuses on the toolbox usage, functionality and implementation. BehaVerify is open source: https://github.com/verivital/behaverify

items.title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
items.summary: A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues. In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.

items.title: Beyond Episodic Recall: Experience-to-Knowledge Evolution for Lifelong Embodied Navigation
items.summary: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.
